Article Title: Asian stocks plunge: Kospi tumbles over 7%, Nikkei sheds 3,000 points as AI-linked shares drag markets
Article Text:
AI trade faces biggest test yet as chip stocks tumble across Asia

Why are global markets falling?

AI stocks face heat

Asian stocks suffered brutal sell-offs on Friday, with Taiwan and South Korea taking the biggest hits as investors turned cautious amid AI fears. The plunge came as Wall Street witnessed its worst session in 18 months, wiping out $2.5 trillion in investor wealth in one of the biggest single-day losses.Asian stock markets witnessed a broad-based sell-off on Friday, with Taiwan and South Korea bearing the brunt of the losses as the rout in technology stocks spread across the region.The sell-off saw Taiwan's weighted index plunge 8%, while South Korea's KOSPI dropped more than 7%. Japan's Nikkei 225 also declined over 3,000 points or 5.95%. The losses extended to Singapore, where the Straits Times index fell 2.20% to 5,180. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was also trading lower during early trading.Technology stocks were among the worst hit, with semiconductor companies facing particularly heavy selling. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged more than 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display also fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as investors dumped technology shares across the country.Japanese technology stocks were not spared either. Semiconductor-related companies witnessed sharp declines, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2% and Tokyo Electron sliding 7.3%.Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.Memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.Taiwan's semiconductor sector also came under intense pressure. Contract chipmaker TSMC slumped 9.6%, while electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry, also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology dropped 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively.Concerns over the future of artificial intelligence-related investments triggered the latest wave of selling in US markets. Investors are worried that the Democratic Party's victory in both chambers of Congress, along with its wins in key gubernatorial races, could slow the expansion of data centres in the US.This has raised concerns about companies involved in AI infrastructure, particularly semiconductor manufacturers and data centre operators, as investors assess whether infrastructure development could face a slowdown.The Nasdaq Composite bore the brunt of the Wall Street sell-off, plunging 5.52% to close at 24,315.00. The index entered correction territory after falling more than 10% below the record level it had reached last month.The S&P 500 declined 4.36% to settle at 7,353.73, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06.Thursday's losses wiped out the previous session's gains, when the Dow had surged more than 1,500 points, marking its best trading day since April 2025. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had also advanced more than 1% each on Wednesday.The technology sell-off on Wall Street was particularly severe for semiconductor companies. Broadcom shares plunged 10%, while Nvidia declined 9%. Software company Oracle also dropped almost 7%.Qualcomm shares fell 9% despite the company reporting earnings that beat estimates, as its outlook for the coming period was weaker than expected.The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) slumped more than 12%, marking its worst trading day since the Covid-19 outbreak in March 2020.Companies in the neocloud segment also witnessed sharp declines. CoreWeave lost almost 10%, while Nebius and Iren fell about 15% and almost 17%, respectively.The selling pressure extended beyond technology stocks, dragging down companies across other sectors. Industrial major Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial company JPMorgan shed 4%. Boeing and Nike shares also fell 2% each.Meanwhile, Brent crude oil prices were trading 1.37% higher at the time of reporting. Dow Jones futures were down 0.59%, pointing to continued weakness in market sentiment.
Article Summary: Taiwan's weighted index plunged 8%, while South Korea's KOSPI dropped more than 7%. Japan's Nikkei 225 also declined over 3,000 points or 5.95%. The losses extended to Singapore, where the Straits Times index fell 2.20% to 5,180. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was also trading lower during early trading.

Article Title: Oil prices bounce back: Brent nears $100 after hitting a more than two-month low
Article Text:
Oil prices inch towards $100 per barrel

Global refining still feeling the impact of Middle East conflict

Russian oil infrastructure attacks add to supply pressures

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think has the biggest impact on crude oil prices? Middle East conflicts US domestic policies Global supply chain issues 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Crude oil prices moved higher again, with Brent approaching the $100-per-barrel mark and US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) also registering gains after the sharp losses recorded earlier in the week. Brent crude was trading at $99.59 per barrel, up $1.30 or 1.32%, while WTI stood at $91.34, gaining $0.82 or 0.91%.The latest recovery comes after Democrats swept control of both the US House of Representatives and Senate, creating a potential legislative check on President Donald Trump’s administration.The rebound follows a sharp correction in the previous sessions. On Wednesday, both oil benchmarks suffered losses of more than 8%, their steepest declines in the period covered by the inputs. Brent shed $8.98, or 8.7%, to close at $94.62 per barrel, while WTI dropped $7.97, or 8.3%, to settle at $88.12. Both ended at their lowest closing levels since August 31.Selling pressure continued on Thursday, pushing Brent below $95 and WTI under $90. Brent futures declined 50 cents, or 0.53%, to $94.12 per barrel, while WTI lost 61 cents, or 0.69%, to $87.51.The fluctuations in crude prices come as the global oil industry continues to deal with the impact of disruptions to supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.The outbreak of conflict in the Middle East weighed heavily on refinery operations during the second quarter of 2026, particularly in countries dependent on crude shipments passing through the strait, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).Global refinery inputs dropped by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d), or 6%, in April-June compared with the preceding quarter, according to data from energy intelligence firm Kpler. Although throughput improved by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter, it remained below earlier levels as refiners adapted to changing trade flows and alternative supply routes.The impact was particularly visible in Asia. China saw refinery inputs fall by 2.1 million b/d in the second quarter, followed by another decline of 0.8 million b/d in the third quarter.India, South Korea and Japan collectively recorded a reduction of more than 1 million b/d in the second quarter. Their combined inputs, however, recovered by 0.8 million b/d in the following quarter.The Middle East also witnessed a slowdown in refining activity as shipping restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz limited exports of refined petroleum products. Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates each recorded a 0.7 million b/d decline in inputs, while Saudi Arabia saw a reduction of 0.3 million b/d and Iran 0.2 million b/d in the second quarter. Together, the four countries recovered 0.4 million b/d in the third quarter.Refinery operations in Russia faced a separate setback, with increased attacks on oil infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict.Russian crude oil inputs declined by 0.6 million b/d in the second quarter and fell by another 0.8 million b/d in the third quarter.The reduced refining activity in Russia, alongside disruptions across Asia and the Middle East, added to the pressure on already tight global diesel supplies. These combined disruptions contributed to diesel prices reaching their highest nominal levels on record in September, the EIA said.The US saw a different trend during the same period. Its refinery inputs rose by 0.5 million b/d in each of the second and third quarters as the country increased refined product exports to make up for shortages in other markets.However, the improvement in refining activity during the third quarter was not enough to restore global throughput to last year's levels. Inputs remained around 5% lower than in the corresponding period of 2025, despite the gradual improvement in crude oil flows.
Article Summary: Brent crude was trading at $99.59 per barrel, up $1.30 or 1.32%. WTI stood at $91.34, gaining $0.82 or 0.91%. The rebound follows a sharp correction in the previous sessions. On Wednesday, both oil benchmarks suffered losses of more than 8%, their steepest declines in the period covered by the inputs.

Article Text:
US stocks crash

Trump blames ‘Dumocrats’ for Wall Street crash

AI trade under pressure

Wall Street suffered a massive selloff on Thursday (local time), wiping out a whopping $2.5 trillion in market value in a single day amid AI fears. The fall came as investors pulled back from technology stocks amid growing concerns over heavy artificial intelligence spending and the possibility of tighter industry regulation. The Nasdaq suffered its worst fall in 18 months while the S&P 500 recorded its worst single-day fall since April 2025.The tech heavy Nasdaq Composite slumped 5.5%, to fall 10% below its recently record high, placing it in correction territory. Nvidia, previously the world’s largest company by market capitalisation, dropped 9.3%, leaving its shares in negative territory for the year. Memory maker SanDisk plunged 22%, while hard drive manufacturer Western Digital lost 17%.The weakness extended across the wider US market, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average, comprising 30 major US companies, falling 1,833 points, or 3.4%, to close at 51,868. The S&P 500 declined between 4.4%, when concerns over US President Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs had rattled markets.All 11 industry sectors of the S&P 500 ended lower, with seven recording losses of at least 2%. Caterpillar shares dropped 6.4%, JPMorgan Chase fell 4.2%, while UnitedHealth and 3M both declined more than 3%, adding to the pressure on the Dow.Meanwhile, Wall Street’s VIX, widely known as its ‘fear index’, surged 61% to its highest level since the early weeks of the Iran war, signalling heightened market volatility.US President Donald Trump has blamed the sharp market sell-off on the outcome of the midterm elections.“The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this,” Trump wrote. “Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry could face tougher scrutiny following the US midterm election results have raised concerns about the pace of investment in the sector.Investors are also positioning for a slower expansion of data centres, putting pressure on chipmakers and companies supplying equipment and infrastructure to the industry.The sharp fall in equities also prompted investors to move towards safer assets, driving demand for US government bonds. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note slipped to its lowest level since September 9.The selloff also spread to Asian markets on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei sliding 6% and South Korea’s Kospi tumbling more than 8% in early trade.

Article Title: Russia's oil and gas tax revenue rises 9.3% in October amid Iran war-driven price surge
Article Text:
Despite the monthly increase, the country's oil and gas tax receipts remained lower for the first 10 months of 2026 (Representative image: Reuters).

Russia's revenue from taxes on oil and gas sales increased 9.3 per cent year on year to 971.2 billion roubles ($11.83 billion) in October, supported by higher crude prices following supply disruptions linked to the Iran war, according to finance ministry data released on Thursday.Despite the monthly increase, the country's oil and gas tax receipts remained lower for the first 10 months of 2026. Revenue between January and October fell 14 per cent from the corresponding period last year to 6.44 trillion roubles, Reuters reported.Oil and gas revenues account for around a fifth of Russia's total federal budget tax receipts and are a major source of funding for its military campaign in Ukraine.Russia's 2026 budget projects oil and gas revenue of 7.58 trillion roubles, below the initial estimate of 8.92 trillion roubles. Total federal budget revenue for the year is projected at 41.182 trillion roubles.Last year, oil and gas revenue in the federal budget fell 24 per cent to 8.48 trillion roubles, its lowest level since 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic affected energy sales.
Article Summary: Russia's revenue from taxes on oil and gas sales increased 9.3 per cent year on year to 971.2 billion roubles ($11.83 billion) in October. Oil and gas revenues account for around a fifth of Russia's total federal budget tax receipts and are a major source of funding for its military campaign in Ukraine.

Article Title: From classroom to billion-dollar fortune: How Chinese siblings struck gold in the stock market
Article Text:
How Chinese siblings struck gold in the stock market

A stock market debut has delivered a billion-dollar glow-up for a former elementary school teacher and his sister in China, turning them into billionaires after shares of their adhesive products company skyrocketed nearly eightfold on their first day of trading.Michael Mai, 62, who once taught at an elementary school in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan, now has an estimated fortune of $2.5 billion following the listing of Crown New Materials Technology on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Tuesday.His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as the company's vice-chairperson, has also made it to the billionaire club, with an estimated net worth of $2 billion.The company, which Mai chairs and leads as CEO, made its stock market debut at 16.98 yuan per share. Its shares subsequently jumped as much as 787%, according to the Shenzhen bourse, mainland China's second-largest stock exchange. The estimated fortunes of the siblings are based on their respective stakes in the business, Forbes reported.Mai is an Australian citizen and permanent resident of Hong Kong. Crown New Materials Technology, founded in 2000, is headquartered in Zhongshan, the same city where he reportedly worked as a teacher.Crown New Materials Technology makes binding agents and other adhesive products used by major brands, including Tesla and Apple. Its products help hold together components used in a variety of retail products, ranging from vehicle roofs to semiconductors in smartphones, according to the company's website.The business has expanded its manufacturing operations to five plants, with four located across China and one in Vietnam, CNN reported.The sharp rally in the company's shares was followed by a correction on Wednesday morning, when they eased to around 77 yuan ($12) apiece. The surge on the previous day had prompted the company to issue a statement asking investors to “invest rationally.”The listing comes against the backdrop of a difficult spell for China's stock markets. Weak consumer spending and concerns about a possible bursting of the AI bubble have weighed on equities in recent months.Key Chinese indexes have fallen more than 20% from their June peaks, entering bear market territory.Beijing responded two weeks ago by injecting $19 billion into exchange-traded funds, according to Bloomberg data. This was its biggest intervention since early 2025, when US President Donald Trump's tariff offensive sent global markets into turmoil.
Article Summary: Michael Mai, 62, once taught at an elementary school in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan. His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as the company's vice- chairperson, has an estimated net worth of $2 billion. Crown New Materials Technology makes binding agents and other adhesive products used by major brands.

Article Title: Anthropic Q3 results: Revenue soars 1,127% to $17 billion, operating loss stands at $567 million
Article Text:
Anthropic's Claude AI now uses a background self-assessment system to identify potentially harmful conversations and flag them for further safety review.

Artificial intelligence company Anthropic’s revenue surged 1,127 per cent year-on-year to $17 billion in the September quarter, but the rapid expansion came with a sharp rise in computing costs, pushing the company into an operating loss.Anthropic reported an operating loss of $567 million for the three months ended September 30, compared with operating income of $974 million in the preceding quarter. Its updated registration statement, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), showed that computing and infrastructure expenses jumped 382 per cent year-on-year to $9.9 billion, as quoted by ANI.The company attributed the pressure in part to the high cost of securing computing capacity through short-term commitments, which are more expensive than longer-term arrangements. It said it continues to face constraints in meeting demand.“We have consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute,” Anthropic said in the filing.The September-quarter operating loss also included around $2 billion in non-cash expenses linked to a donation-matching programme. On an adjusted basis, operating income stood at $2.5 billion, compared with $2.2 billion in the June quarter.Adjusted operating margin, however, narrowed to 15 per cent from 19 per cent.Anthropic expects its reliance on more expensive short-term computing arrangements to continue in the near term. “We expect our use of short-term compute to continue to increase in the near term,” it said, indicating that margins could remain under pressure as the company scales up to meet demand.For the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached $33.2 billion, against $2.5 billion in the corresponding period last year. Operating loss narrowed to $1.3 billion from $5.2 billion.The company reported a net loss of $23.3 billion for the September quarter and $104 billion for the first nine months of the year. Much of the nine-month loss was driven by a $94.3 billion non-cash charge arising from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and other financial instruments, primarily reflecting an increase in their valuation.Anthropic’s aggregate commitments to purchase and lease computing capacity stood at $895.4 billion, of which $447.5 billion is expected to fall due before December 2030. The scale of these obligations underscores the capital-intensive nature of building and operating advanced AI systems.Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic is seeking to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. The filing does not yet specify the number of shares to be offered or the price range. The proposed offering will include newly issued shares as well as shares held by existing shareholders.
Article Summary: Anthropic reported an operating loss of $567 million for the three months ended September 30, compared with operating income of $974 million in the preceding quarter. The company attributed the pressure in part to the high cost of securing computing capacity through short-term commitments, which are more expensive than longer-term arrangements.

Article Title: Oil prices edge higher after reported US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island, reviving supply concerns
Article Text:
Brent crude rose 0.5% to $105.25 a barrel, while WTI gained 0.5% to $96.93.

Oil prices edged higher in early Asian trade on Tuesday after reports of a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island raised fresh concerns about the conflict, even as diplomatic efforts to end the war continued.Brent crude futures rose 48 cents, or 0.5%, to $105.25 a barrel by 0104 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 47 cents, or 0.5%, to $96.93.The gains came a day after Brent slumped 7.63%, shedding $8.66 to settle at $104.77 a barrel, as markets weighed the possibility of progress in efforts to end the conflict.However, reports of fresh military action have put the focus back on the risk of further escalation. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials, that American forces had struck Iran's Qeshm Island. Some officials described the strikes as defensive, intended to prevent Iran from targeting commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.The waterway remains central to concerns over global energy supplies. Before the conflict began in late February, it carried around a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas.The sharp reduction in shipping traffic since then has kept supply risks elevated.At the same time, both sides have indicated that the door to negotiations remains open. Iran said contacts with Washington were continuing after talks with Qatari mediators ended without a breakthrough, although revised proposals were put forward.US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, cast doubt on whether he would resume threatened military strikes and said an agreement with Tehran was still possible. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government certain powers to pursue peace talks.The competing signals have left oil markets balancing the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough against the threat of renewed military action. Brent had already climbed to a six-month high at the end of October amid concerns over an escalation in the Middle East.High fuel prices are also adding to pressure on Trump to bring the conflict to an end, with the war emerging as a key factor behind rising gasoline costs in the US.Separately, Washington is scheduled to host Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 for discussions on ending the war in Ukraine, post-war security arrangements and de-escalation.
Article Summary: Brent crude futures rose 48 cents, or 0.5%, to $105.25 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 47 cents to $96.93. Gains came a day after Brent slumped 7.63%, shedding $8.66 to settle at $104.77. Reports of fresh military action put the focus back on the risk of further escalation.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
